title: Why Far Signals Ride the Blood

scenes.tts: Cut every nerve to a loop of a dog's gut, then drip weak acid onto its lining. The pancreas still secretes its juice. It sits in a different part of the abdomen, and the leading view said the gut instructs it by nerve. But no wire joins the two organs now. What carried the message?
scenes.visual: A gut loop and a pancreas inside the abdomen. A bundle of nerves between them is cut (red bar, the halves slide apart). Orange acid drips on the gut and green juice drips from the pancreas anyway. The cut nerves are replaced by a dashed path of question-mark boxes.
scenes.narration: Cut every nerve to a loop of a dog's gut, then drip weak acid onto its lining. The pancreas still secretes its juice. It sits in a different part of the abdomen, and the leading view said the gut instructs it by nerve. But no wire joins the two organs now. What carried the message?

scenes.tts: The answer was a chemical, later named secretin. Acid released it from the gut lining, and the blood carried it to the pancreas. An extract of the lining, filtered and injected into a vein, made the pancreas secrete even more. But molecules can also drift on their own. So why ride the blood at all?
scenes.visual: The question-mark boxes become one yellow dot, labelled chemical, then secretin. Acid drips on the gut and yellow dots leave it, ride a teal vessel to the pancreas, and juice drips. An extract is injected into the vessel and more juice falls. The vessel fades, the dots drift out of the gut in all directions, and a large question mark replaces the vessel.
scenes.narration: The answer was a chemical, later named secretin. Acid released it from the gut lining, and the blood carried it to the pancreas. An extract of the lining, filtered and injected into a vein, made the pancreas secrete even more. But molecules can also drift on their own. So why ride the blood at all?

scenes.tts: That drift is called diffusion. A diffusing molecule is not heading anywhere. It wanders. The typical time to wander a distance grows with the square of that distance. So diffusion punishes distance: a far target waits much longer than a near one.
scenes.visual: A source releases a cloud of dots that wander; one dot leaves a zig-zag trail. A near target and a far target appear. A gold time bar grows as the cloud reaches the near target, then grows far longer before the far target fills.
scenes.narration: That drift is called diffusion. A diffusing molecule is not heading anywhere. It wanders. The typical time to wander a distance grows with the square of that distance. So diffusion punishes distance: a far target waits much longer than a near one.

scenes.tts: Take a small molecule in water, and change only the distance. It crosses a synaptic gap, twenty nanometers wide, in a fraction of a microsecond. It crosses a millimeter in about eight minutes. It crosses a centimeter in about fourteen hours. The centimeter is only ten times farther than the millimeter, yet it costs hours instead of minutes.

It crosses a millimeter in about 8 minutes. It crosses a centimeter in about 14 hours. The centimeter is only ten times farther than the millimeter, yet it costs hours instead of minutes.
scenes.visual: A plot of time against distance, both in tenfold steps, with the curve time = distance squared over 2D computed from the equation. Three gold points arrive in turn: the 20 nm gap, the millimeter and the centimeter, each labelled with its time. A bracket marks the tenfold step from millimeter to centimeter and the jump from minutes to hours.

It crosses a millimeter in about 8 minutes. It crosses a centimeter in about 14 hours. The centimeter is only ten times farther than the millimeter, yet it costs hours instead of minutes.

scenes.tts: Past a few hundred micrometers, diffusion cannot deliver a message that must act within a minute. So a gland releases its hormone into the blood, which circulates around the body in about a minute. Fast local signals do the opposite. A nerve cell releases its message into a gap only tens of nanometers wide. The message arrives almost at once, though some spills out to nearby cells.
scenes.visual: A gland and a distant target: dots wander near the gland, a clock sweeps, a red cross marks the empty gap. A teal loop of blood appears; dots ride it once round in one clock turn and the target lights green. The loop shrinks to a corner. A nerve cell and a receiving cell sit across a tiny gap; dots cross at once and the receiver lights green while some dots spill out to a nearby cell.
scenes.narration: Past a few hundred micrometers, diffusion cannot deliver a message that must act within a minute. So a gland releases its hormone into the blood, which circulates around the body in about a minute. Fast local signals do the opposite. A nerve cell releases its message into a gap only tens of nanometers wide. The message arrives almost at once, though some spills out to nearby cells.

scenes.tts: The extract reached every organ in the dog, and the pancreas poured out juice. A signal does not choose its audience. The receiver does. Epinephrine, a hormone, makes liver cells break down glycogen, fat cells break down fat, and the heart beat harder. So keep this rule: far messages ride the blood, and the receptor decides who answers.
scenes.visual: A vessel runs over four organs. Yellow dots reach all of them; the pancreas releases juice, while the other organs are labelled response unknown. The row becomes a liver cell, a fat cell and a heart cell, each with a cup that catches epinephrine and answers in its own way, and a fourth cell with no cup that ignores it.
